title: Six WWI Soldiers of Queen's Royal West Surrey Regiment Buried at Tyne Cot After DNA Identification
detail: On June 10, 2026, the remains of six First World War soldiers of the 2/4th Battalion, Queen's Royal West Surrey Regiment were buried with full military honours at the Commonwealth War Graves Commission's Tyne Cot Cemetery near Zonnebeke, Belgium, 108 years after they died together in a shell strike near Gheluwe on October 6, 1918. Privates Horace Cook (Matching, Essex), Frederick Martin (London), Charles Russell (London), Thomas Whitaker (Bradford, West Yorkshire), Courtney Hart (Northampton) and Joseph Turnley (Bristol) were discovered by archaeologists in 2020 still wearing their regimental shoulder titles and equipment for repairing a Lewis Gun. The Ministry of Defence's Joint Casualty and Compassionate Centre (JCCC), known as the 'MOD War Detectives', traced descendants of each man to obtain comparative DNA samples, confirming positive matches for all six. A postcard from Bradford carried by Private Whitaker helped researchers reconnect estranged branches of his family. Descendants including Paul Turnley (great-nephew of Joseph Turnley) and Joe Whitaker (great-great-nephew of Thomas Whitaker) attended the service, with a bearer party provided by 1st Battalion The Princess of Wales's Royal Regiment.

media.caption: Burial service for six Queen's Royal West Surrey Regiment soldiers at Tyne Cot Cemetery, Belgium, June 10, 2026

title: Hill 70 Memorial Park Inaugurates Brutinel Visitors Pavilion, Completing Canadian WWI Battlefield Site
detail: On June 10, 2026, Hill 70 Memorial Park in Loos-en-Gohelle, France, formally inaugurated the Brutinel Visitors Pavilion, the last major structure to be completed at the site commemorating the Battle of Hill 70 (August 1917) — the first major operation planned and commanded entirely by Canadian officers, under Lieutenant-General Sir Arthur Currie, in which more than 100,000 Canadians fought. The pavilion is named for Brigadier-General Raymond Brutinel, a French-born Canadian officer who founded the Canadian Automobile Machine Gun Brigade, one of the first motorized machine-gun formations in the British Empire. The ceremony included media accreditation from midday, an official dedication at 13:25 local time, and a tour of the memorial park, marking the culmination of a multi-year effort by the Hill 70 Memorial Project to complete the battlefield site.

media.caption: The Brutinel Visitors Pavilion at Hill 70 Memorial Park, Loos-en-Gohelle, France
